description: I'm sure there are tax implications, and other things to consider. I don't know where to start.
reference_answer:
In short - if you can't get the job without incorporating, then incorporate!

Some clients will require you to be incorporated (which is why I did it 10 years ago). Essentially, for them, it's a way of distancing themselves from you to ensure they are not responsible for any monies if you don't pay your taxes. For you, there is also this idea of distancing company assets from your personal assets. If they are not requiring you to incorporate, you can simply act as a sole proprietorship.

A good place to start reading up could be the sites below (for Canada/Ontario):

[Canada Business](http://www.canadabusiness.ca)

<http://sbinfocanada.about.com/>

[http://sbinfocanada.about.com/od/incorporation/Incorporating\_A\_Business\_In\_Canada.htm](http://sbinfocanada.about.com/od/incorporation/Incorporating%5FA%5FBusiness%5FIn%5FCanada.htm)

<http://sbinfocanada.about.com/cs/startup/a/incorporatadv.htm>

When I registered, I simply bought a book at Grand&Toy, with all the required forms for Ontario. These forms would also be available at a local Government service centre. You walk in, give the government money, and shortly thereafter you are incorporated.

There are a number of others things that are required (having a minutes book, writing resolutions, creating shares, setting up a bank account, etc) - all discussed in the guide

For Ontario you can start here:
<http://www.ontario.ca/en/services_for_business/index.htm>

At a high level, there are some costs for being incorporated, and some tax savings. At a minimum, costs would include:

- Incorporation costs - from memory this is a few hundred dollars
- Name Search around $50 (you are not required to pick a name, and can simply use the numbered company from the incorporation, so this is optional)
- Bank Account in the business's name (RBC is good for new companies as they have the lowest charges currently - see <http://www.redflagdeals.com> forums for a more indepth discussion.

You may need the help of an account to help set things up, but it's quite easy to maintain all the records, etc that are required.

Some other minor things I enjoy are writing myself expense cheques so that I get money back immediately (and effectively only pay 60% of the cost after writing it off in the company). I can decide how much to pay myself and push income from year to year.
synthetic_response:
It is completely normal to feel overwhelmed when transitioning into contract work. You are moving from a world where your employer handles the "back office" to a world where you are the CEO, HR, and Accounting departments all at once. Taking a moment to pause and learn the landscape is the best way to prevent the financial mistakes you’re worried about.

Let’s break this down into four manageable steps to help you decide which path is right for you.

### 1. The Two Main Paths: Sole Proprietorship vs. Incorporation
Think of this choice like **renting vs. buying a home**.
*   **Sole Proprietorship (Renting):** It is simple, cheap, and requires very little paperwork. You and the business are the same "legal entity." Just as renting is easier to start and stop, a sole proprietorship is the default for most freelancers.
*   **Incorporation (Buying):** This creates a separate "legal person" (the corporation). Like buying a house, it offers more protection and long-term benefits, but it comes with higher upfront costs (legal fees), maintenance (yearly filings), and complexity.

**When is incorporation necessary?** Usually only if a client *insists* on it to protect themselves, or if your work carries a high risk of being sued, as the corporation acts as a shield for your personal assets.

### 2. Understanding the Tax Differences
The way the government views your money changes depending on your structure:

*   **Employee:** Your boss takes taxes out before you see your paycheck.
*   **Sole Proprietor:** You receive the full amount from your client. At the end of the year, you report this as personal income. You can deduct business expenses (like a home office or laptop), but you pay your personal tax rate on every dollar you earn.
*   **Corporation:** The business is taxed at a lower "Corporate Tax Rate." You only pay personal income tax on the money you choose to pay yourself out of the corporation. This is great for "tax deferral"—if the business makes $150,000 but you only need $60,000 to live on, you leave the rest in the company and avoid paying high personal taxes on that extra $90,000.

### 3. Practical Steps and Costs
If you decide to incorporate, it isn't just a one-time fee. It involves:
*   **Setup:** Filing "Articles of Incorporation" and performing a name search (approx. $200–$500+).
*   **Administration:** You must keep a "Minute Book," issue shares, and open a separate business bank account.
*   **Compliance:** You will need to file a separate corporate tax return every year, which usually requires hiring an accountant ($1,500–$3,000 per year).

### 4. Assessing Your Situation
To decide, ask yourself these two questions:
1.  **How much will I earn?** If you are a freelance graphic designer earning $50,000, the $2,500 in accounting fees will eat up your profits. A sole proprietorship is likely better. If you are a consultant earning $160,000, the tax savings of a corporation will far outweigh the costs.
2.  **What is my risk?** If you are giving high-stakes legal or engineering advice, you may want the liability protection of a corporation.

### Summary and Next Steps
Don't feel pressured to incorporate on day one unless a contract requires it. You can always start as a sole proprietor and "grow into" a corporation later as your income increases.

**Your Homework:**
1.  **Check your contracts:** Do your clients require you to be incorporated?
2.  **Estimate your net income:** Will you have "extra" money to leave in a business bank account, or do you need every cent for living expenses?
3.  **Consult a professional:** Once you have an estimate of your earnings, spend one hour with a CPA (Chartered Professional Accountant). They can run the math to show you exactly at what dollar amount incorporation starts saving you money.

You’ve got this! Taking it one step at a time makes the process much less daunting. Do you have a rough idea of what your annual contract income might look like?
